attempts.raw_response: Yet neither dared to speak the words aloud, for the tree was all that remained of their grandfather’s garden, a silent witness to summers long past. The memory of its sweet fruit hung heavy in the air, contrasting sharply with the barren branches that scraped against the grey sky like skeletal fingers. Ned watched as Tom kicked at the dry earth beneath the trunk, his small face twisted in frustration. They wanted warmth, they wanted change, but cutting it down felt like erasing a part of themselves. The house loomed behind them, dark and cold, while the tree stood defiantly between them and the future, a stubborn relic refusing to yield to the relentless advance of winter.

pair.human_continuation:
"How I wish," exclaimed Tom, "that we had another to put in its place!"

"So do I," rejoined Ned; "but apricot-trees, I believe, are very dear to
buy. A gardener my father used to work for, and who is now dead, gave me
this. I fear there is no chance of our ever getting another."

"How I do wish I was rich!" cried Tom; "I would give you an
apricot-tree, and all manner of things besides. I should like to be as
rich as our Squire best; but it would do to be as rich as Farmer
Tomkyns. Oh, if I had only half as many sheep, and pigs, and cows, and
haystacks, as he has, how happy I should be!
pair.prefix:
Ned could not help sighing when he saw his grandmother
suffering from the cold, and recollected that she had no cloak to keep
her warm, and would have none all the winter.

He sometimes sighed, too, as he looked at the apricot-tree, whose
branches were now dead and withering; and so did Tom. Both the boys
agreed that it had better be cut down, and taken away entirely.
